newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU - and Britain - agree discrimination measure.
newsitem.headline: EU - and Britain - agree discrimination measure.

text.p: European Union social affairs ministers agreed a measure on Friday to make it easier for employees to win sex discrimination cases after negotiations that included Britain for the first time.

"Today marks a new chapter in Britain's relations with Europe," David Blunkett, employment secretary in the new Labour government, said in a statement. "No longer will there be an empty UK negotiating chair when the (EU) considers social policy."
The former Conservative government did not take part in previous talks on the legislation because of its "opt-out" from some EU workplace regulations under the Maastricht Treaty's "social chapter".
But Prime Minister Tony Blair's Labour government has agreed to sign up to the social chapter, which will be incorporated into a new treaty agreed at a summit in Amsterdam last week.
Blunkett was one of three representatives who attended the Luxembourg meeting.
The sex-discrimination directive, which must be approved by the European Parliament before final adoption, aims to ensure that employers share the burden of proof when they are sued.
It says workers must first establish before a court or other competent authority "facts from which it can be presumed that there has been direct or indirect discrimination".
The employer would then have to prove that it had not violated the principle of equal treatment.

Britain cannot play a formal role in debates under the social chapter until the new treaty is ratified. However, EU leaders agreed that other countries would take account of its views in adopting legislation.

In this case, they accepted Britain's request for language guaranteeing that its own system of handling sex-discrimination suits through industrial tribunals meets the terms of the legislation, officials said.
The ministers agreed the text after resolving a dispute with the European Commission over the scope of the directive.
The Commission -- unlike most EU states -- wanted it to apply to EU rules on social security and self-employed people, as well as those on issues such as equal pay, hiring and promotions.
The ministers agreed that the Commission should address the scope in a report it has been asked to prepare on the directive two years after it takes force on January 1, 2001.
